title: The Paper Clutter System for People Who Hate Filing
description: An easy paper clutter system with 3 decisions and zero filing marathons, plus 7 Amazon finds for mail, bills and school forms.
intro:
Paper is the sneakiest clutter there is. It arrives every single day, it's flat so it stacks invisibly, and every piece needs a tiny decision. Bill? Junk? Permission slip due tomorrow? Coupon you'll never use?

For our brains, that means paper piles up on every flat surface until something important gets lost in there. (Ask us about the parking ticket.)

Here's a paper system built for people who will never, ever enjoy filing.

sections.heading: The system: 3 decisions, not 30
sections.body:
Every piece of paper that comes into your home gets one of three decisions, the moment you touch it:

1. **Toss** it (recycling or shred).
2. **Act** on it (it needs you to do something: pay, sign, call, RSVP).
3. **Keep** it (you need it for records, but it doesn't need action).

That's the whole system. No 20-category filing cabinet.

sections.heading: Step 1: Open mail at the recycling bin
sections.body:
Put a slim recycling bin exactly where mail enters the house, next to the launch pad or kitchen counter. Open mail standing there. Most of it is junk, and junk goes straight in the bin.

If you have a shredder, put it right there too. Sensitive junk goes in the shredder immediately, not in a "to shred" pile that lives forever.

sections.heading: Step 2: One ACT spot everyone can see
sections.body:
Anything that needs action goes in one visible place: a wall pocket, a clipboard or a fridge file pocket. Not a drawer. A drawer is where action items go to die.

Bills can go in a bill organizer with a pocket for each week, so you see what's due next without digging.

sections.heading: Step 3: A simple KEEP box
sections.body:
For papers you need to keep, use one file box with hanging folders and only a handful of broad categories:

- Home (lease or mortgage, utilities)
- Money (taxes, bank)
- Medical and insurance
- Car
- Kids (one folder each)
- Manuals and warranties (or a binder with sheet protectors)

Broad categories mean fewer decisions. You're not trying to find it in two seconds. You're trying to find it at all.

sections.heading: Step 4: Weekly 10-minute paper session
sections.body:
Pick a day. Friday afternoon works for a lot of people. Set a timer for ten minutes:

- Go through the ACT spot. Do the quick ones, calendar the rest.
- Drop anything done into KEEP or recycling.
- Check the bill organizer for next week.

Pair it with something nice, like a coffee or a favorite show. Paper is boring. Bribe yourself.

sections.heading: Kids' school papers
sections.body:
School papers are their own beast. Give each kid a clipboard on the wall. Forms that need signing get clipped on top. Art gets displayed for a week, then photographed and recycled, or saved in one "best of the year" folder.

Keeping every drawing isn't love. Keeping the best ones and enjoying them is.

outro:
Toss, act or keep. Three decisions, one bin by the door and ten minutes a week.

Our ebook *The Messy Brain Home Reset* has a dedicated paper day with a printable version of this whole flow if you want some guided help.
